## Introduction and reading guide

General combining ability (GCA) describes a parent's average performance
in crosses with a specified set of mates.
Specific combining ability (SCA) describes how a particular cross
departs from the performance predicted by the two parents' GCA effects
[@sprague1942General].
Both depend on the parents and crossing design used to define them.

This vignette uses a small, complete factorial crossing design between
two sets of inbred diploid parents.
It distinguishes the cross means returned by AlphaSimR from centered GCA
effects and SCA deviations.
The companion `vignette("traits")` introduces trait specification,
`vignette("QuanGen")` explains genetic values and their variances, and
`vignette("GeneticRecombination")` explains inheritance during crossing.

| If you want to understand... | Start with... |
|:--|:--|
| What GCA and SCA mean | [A decomposition of cross performance](#decomposition) |
| What `calcGCA()` returns | [A complete crossing example](#crossing) |
| How testers affect GCA | [Changing the tester set](#testers) |
| How GCA and SCA contribute to variation | [Variance among crosses](#variance) |
| How to use combining ability in selection | [Selection and prediction](#selection) |

Run the examples in order.
All simulations use explicit `simParam` arguments so that they can
coexist with other examples in an R session.

## A decomposition of cross performance {#decomposition}

Let $M_{ij}$ be the mean genetic value of offspring from female parent
$i$ and male parent $j$.
In a complete factorial design, every female is crossed with every male.
Giving each cross equal weight, define:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu &= \operatorname{mean}_{i,j}(M_{ij}), \\
g_{F_i} &= \operatorname{mean}_j(M_{ij}) - \mu, \\
g_{M_j} &= \operatorname{mean}_i(M_{ij}) - \mu, \\
s_{ij} &= M_{ij} - \mu - g_{F_i} - g_{M_j}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The centered GCA effects are $g_{F_i}$ and $g_{M_j}$, and the SCA
deviation is $s_{ij}$.
Thus:

$$M_{ij} = \mu + g_{F_i} + g_{M_j} + s_{ij}.$$

The GCA effects average to zero within each parental set.
The SCA matrix has zero row and column means.
A positive SCA deviation means that a cross performs better than
predicted by the two GCA effects; it does not necessarily mean that the
cross has the highest genetic value.

This is a decomposition across crosses.
It is not the same as the breeding value and non-additive deviation
decomposition of individuals returned by `genParam()`.
In particular, SCA is not generally equal to `dd()` or `nd()`, and GCA
effects should not automatically be equated with `bv()` from either
parental population.
The reference mates and centering differ.
Non-additive genotypic effects can influence both average cross
performance and cross-specific departures.

## A complete crossing example {#crossing}

We create six female and six male inbred lines, all drawn from the same
founder population.
These are two sets of parents, not simulated heterotic groups.
The trait includes additive and dominance effects.
Because the diploid parents are fully inbred, each cross has a single F1
genotype, so its genetic value also represents its family mean.

```{r parents-and-crosses}
set.seed(1942)
founders = quickHaplo(nInd=12, nChr=2, segSites=40, inbred=TRUE)
SPgca = SimParam$new(founders)
SPgca$nThreads = 1L
SPgca$addTraitAD(nQtlPerChr=20, mean=10, meanDD=0.8, varDD=0.2)
parents = newPop(founders, simParam=SPgca)
females = parents[1:6]
males = parents[7:12]

hybrids = hybridCross(females, males, crossPlan="testcross",
                      returnHybridPop=TRUE, simParam=SPgca)
combining = calcGCA(hybrids, use="gv")
```

`returnHybridPop=TRUE` calculates hybrid values without retaining their
full genotypes.
It is appropriate here because both sets of parents are fully inbred.
Use `returnHybridPop=FALSE` when offspring genotypes are needed, for
example for subsequent crossing or genomic prediction.

### Means returned by calcGCA

For this balanced design, `calcGCA()` returns:

| Output | Meaning |
|:--|:--|
| `GCAf` | Mean cross performance for each female parent |
| `GCAm` | Mean cross performance for each male parent |
| `SCA` | Mean performance of each female-by-male cross |

Despite their names, these outputs retain the overall mean: `SCA` is
**not** the centered SCA deviation $s_{ij}$.
We calculate the centered quantities below.
The `id` column identifies parents or crosses, and `Trait1` contains
values for the first trait.
Cross IDs join the mother and father IDs with an underscore.

```{r combining-means}
combining$GCAf
combining$GCAm
head(combining$SCA)
```

### Centered GCA effects and SCA deviations

Arrange the genetic values by parental identity, rather than relying on
the order in which the crosses were generated.

```{r centered-combining-ability}
M = matrix(NA_real_, nrow=nInd(females), ncol=nInd(males),
           dimnames=list(females@id, males@id))
rowIndex = match(hybrids@mother, females@id)
colIndex = match(hybrids@father, males@id)
M[cbind(rowIndex, colIndex)] = gv(hybrids)[, 1]
stopifnot(!anyNA(M))

crossMean = mean(M)
gcaFemale = rowMeans(M) - crossMean
gcaMale = colMeans(M) - crossMean
expected = crossMean + outer(gcaFemale, gcaMale, "+")
sca = M - expected

round(gcaFemale, 3)
round(gcaMale, 3)
round(sca, 3)

# Verify centering and reconstruction before rounding.
stopifnot(max(abs(rowMeans(sca))) < 1e-10,
          max(abs(colMeans(sca))) < 1e-10,
          max(abs(M - (expected + sca))) < 1e-10)

# Check the relationship to calcGCA's uncentered output.
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(
  unname(rowMeans(M)),
  combining$GCAf$Trait1[match(females@id, combining$GCAf$id)]
)))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(
  unname(colMeans(M)),
  combining$GCAm$Trait1[match(males@id, combining$GCAm$id)]
)))
crossIds = paste(hybrids@mother, hybrids@father, sep="_")
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(
  gv(hybrids)[, 1],
  combining$SCA$Trait1[match(crossIds, combining$SCA$id)],
  check.attributes=FALSE
)))
```

Each cell in `sca` is the residual after accounting for both parents'
average cross performance.
Dominance permits such departures even though every offspring within a
cross has the same genotype.
SCA therefore does not require segregation within a family.

## Changing the tester set {#testers}

GCA is defined relative to a set of mates.
Here we keep the female lines fixed and compare their mean performance
against all six males with that against the first three males.
`setPhenoGCA()` makes the testcrosses and averages their performance for
each candidate parent.

```{r tester-comparison}
allTesters = setPhenoGCA(females, testers=males, use="gv",
                         inbred=TRUE, onlyPheno=TRUE, simParam=SPgca)
fewerTesters = setPhenoGCA(females, testers=males[1:3], use="gv",
                           inbred=TRUE, onlyPheno=TRUE, simParam=SPgca)
stopifnot(max(abs(allTesters[, 1] - rowMeans(M))) < 1e-10,
          max(abs(fewerTesters[, 1] - rowMeans(M[, 1:3]))) < 1e-10)

round(cbind(
  mean_all=allTesters[, 1],
  mean_subset=fewerTesters[, 1],
  gca_all=allTesters[, 1] - mean(allTesters[, 1]),
  gca_subset=fewerTesters[, 1] - mean(fewerTesters[, 1])
), 3)
```

Both the mean and the centered GCA effects can change when testers
change; rankings can also change.
A parent therefore has combining ability relative to a specified tester
set, rather than a single GCA that applies to every breeding population.

With `onlyPheno=FALSE`, `setPhenoGCA()` returns the candidate population
with these testcross means stored in its phenotype slot.
The candidates' own genetic values are unchanged.
The `inbred=TRUE` option requires both candidates and testers to be
fully inbred.
With `inbred=FALSE`, the function samples one offspring per
candidate-tester pair and averages those sampled values.
Segregation therefore adds sampling variation even with `use="gv"`.
The `reps` argument reduces phenotypic error; it does not increase the
number of offspring sampled per pair.
To average several offspring per cross, generate them with
`makeCross2()` and summarize their values explicitly.

## Variance among crosses {#variance}

For the complete, equally weighted design above, the centered GCA and
SCA contributions are orthogonal across crosses.
Consequently:

$$\operatorname{Var}(M_{ij}) =
\operatorname{Var}(g_{F_i}) + \operatorname{Var}(g_{M_j}) +
\operatorname{Var}(s_{ij}).$$

We use population variances, dividing by the number of values, as in
`vignette("QuanGen")`.

```{r combining-variances}
populationVariance = function(x) mean((x - mean(x))^2)
components = c(femaleGCA=populationVariance(gcaFemale),
               maleGCA=populationVariance(gcaMale),
               SCA=populationVariance(as.vector(sca)))
round(c(components, total=sum(components),
        observed=populationVariance(as.vector(M))), 4)
stopifnot(abs(sum(components) -
                populationVariance(as.vector(M))) < 1e-10)
```

These are descriptive variances for the chosen crosses, not estimates of
universal GCA or SCA variance components.
The simple sum relies on the complete design and equal weights.
In an incomplete or unbalanced design, row and column means alone do not
provide this orthogonal partition.
`calcGCA()` uses an additive female-plus-male model to adjust parental
means for unbalanced designs; its `SCA` output remains the observed
cross means.
Each offspring record has equal weight in that fit, while fitted
parental means average equally over the opposite set of parents.
Incomplete designs need to be connected to identify parental effects.

The current `calcGCA()` implementation has a limitation when one side
contains only one parent and the other contains multiple parents:
repeated records per cross are not averaged for the latter parental set.
Aggregate to one record per cross before using that special case.
The complete six-by-six example above is unaffected.

Estimating variance components from noisy trials requires an appropriate
statistical model and an informative design.

## Selection and prediction {#selection}

The examples use `use="gv"` to expose the simulated genetic values.
Using phenotypes introduces environmental variation.
For example, `setPhenoGCA(..., use="pheno", varE=..., reps=...)`
averages simulated testcross phenotypes rather than genetic values.
Specify the trial error and replication to represent the intended
testing scheme.

For choosing parents, compare their average performance against the
relevant tester population.
For choosing a commercial hybrid, compare its total predicted
performance, including the mean, both GCA effects, and SCA.
Selecting the largest SCA residual alone can overlook crosses with
better total performance.

The genomic prediction functions `RRBLUP_GCA()` and `RRBLUP_SCA()` fit
marker models to hybrid data; they do not simply tabulate cross means as
`calcGCA()` does.
The former fits separate parental-origin additive marker effects, and
the latter also includes dominance effects.
Both require training offspring with genotypes and retained parental
origin, so use `returnHybridPop=FALSE` when generating those offspring.
With `setEBV(..., value="gv")`, both models predict total hybrid
genetic values; the SCA model does not return a centered SCA deviation
through this option.
See `vignette("GenomicSelection")` for model choice and prediction.

As an extension, replace the inbred parents with outbred parents and
simulate several offspring per cross using `makeCross2()`.
Cross means will then be estimated from segregating offspring.
Compare variation among cross means with variation within crosses,
keeping this family partition distinct from the GCA/SCA partition among
cross means.
